title: Stari Grad for Seniors: Accessibility Guide 2027
metaDescription: Senior travel guide to Stari Grad, Hvar: ferry access, flat waterfront walks, step-free limits, heat, costs in euros and practical tips for 2027.
content:
## Is Stari Grad Good for Seniors?

Yes, with conditions. Stari Grad is one of the oldest continuously inhabited towns in Europe, founded by Greek settlers from Paros in 384 BC. It is small enough to cover on foot, and the terrain is gentler than in Hvar Town, where the fortress hill and stepped lanes limit mobility. The main obstacles are uneven and polished stone paving, a lack of ramps in historic buildings, and summer heat.

A short trip suits people who can walk 1–2 km at a slow pace with rest stops. Wheelchair users and walker users can manage the waterfront and many cafés, but should plan around cobbles and steps elsewhere.

## Getting to Stari Grad Step by Step

### By Ferry from Split

Jadrolinija runs the car ferry (line 635) all year, with up to 7 sailings a day in summer. The crossing takes 1 h 50 min. A 2026 adult fare is €5.90 in low season and €8.40 in the high season, which runs roughly from late May to late September. The ferry has a lower deck and lounge seating, and the vehicle ramp avoids stairs at boarding. Staff on the ship can usually assist on request, but tell the ticket office beforehand.

The direct Split–Hvar Town catamaran costs about €25 in high season, but it lands 20 km from Stari Grad and adds a transfer. Choose the Stari Grad ferry if Stari Grad is the destination.

### From the Port to the Old Town

The ferry port lies about 1.5 km from the old town centre, which is a 20-minute walk for most people. Seniors with luggage should take a taxi (typically €8–15). Ask the accommodation to arrange pickup before arrival. Ferries at night and early morning (a 01:30 and a 05:00 departure from Split exist) arrive when taxis are scarce, so pre-book.

## Walking and Mobility in Stari Grad

### Flat Routes

The waterfront (Riva) and the bay promenade are close to level and make the easiest walks. The promenade running around the bay is roughly 2 km, with benches and shade from pines in places. The old town's lanes are narrow and mostly flat, with limestone paving worn smooth by centuries of use.

### Surface Problems

Polished limestone becomes slippery when wet or dusty. Wear shoes with rubber soles, and use a walking stick with a rubber tip. Wheeled walkers work on the Riva but struggle on cobbled side lanes. Few shops and restaurants have ramps; most cafés on the waterfront are at street level.

### Tvrdalj and Other Sights

Tvrdalj, the 16th-century fortified house of poet Petar Hektorović, has a central fishpond and a garden. Entry is €5, cash only. Hours are reported as roughly 10:00–14:00 in many listings, and evening hours vary by season, so check at the door. Wheelchair access is limited because of thresholds and uneven surfaces, but the courtyard and pond can be viewed with a slow walk from the gate. Visits take 15–45 minutes.

The Dominican Monastery and its small museum, and the Stari Grad Museum in the old town, are short, low-effort stops. Both involve stairs or thresholds, so ask before arriving.

### The Stari Grad Plain

The Stari Grad Plain, a UNESCO World Heritage agricultural landscape of Greek origin, begins at the edge of town. Flat gravel and dry-stone lanes allow a 1–3 km walk past vineyards and olive groves. Mornings are best. Wheelchair use is difficult on loose gravel.

## Where to Stay

Choose accommodation within 300 m of the Riva to avoid the 1.5 km port-to-town stretch on foot every day. Ground-floor apartments and rooms with a lift are scarce, so confirm on booking: ask for a ground-floor unit, a walk-in shower with no step, and air conditioning. Heritage Hotel Antique is a well-known option in the old town, but historic buildings seldom offer fully step-free rooms, so confirm room details directly.

## Best Time to Visit

| Season | Typical conditions | Senior suitability |
|---|---|---|
| April–June | Mild, 18–26°C | Best |
| July–August | Hot, often above 30°C | Difficult midday |
| September–October | Warm sea, 20–27°C | Best |
| November–March | Quiet, many places closed | Limited services |

The ferry sells out in July and August for vehicles, so seniors travelling with a car should book ahead and arrive early at the Split port.

## Opinion: Skip the Hvar Town Day Trip

Most visitors assume a first Hvar visit must include Hvar Town. For seniors, that is the wrong priority. Hvar Town is crowded, steep around the fortress and expensive, and the climb to the Spanish Fortress is a poor trade for most knees. Stari Grad gives the same Venetian-era stone streets, waterfront cafés and sea views with less effort and lower prices. Spend the saved energy on the Stari Grad Plain instead.

## Health, Safety and Practical Tips

- Stari Grad has a health centre and a pharmacy. The nearest full hospital is in Split, reached by ferry, so carry prescriptions and a printed medication list.
- Carry euros in cash. Tvrdalj and some small shops accept cash only. ATMs are available in town.
- Eat lunch early. Many restaurants close between lunch and dinner service in shoulder season.
- Rest 13:00–17:00 in summer, then walk the Riva after 18:00.
- Drink water often. Croatian tap water is safe to drink.
- Travel insurance with medical cover is advisable. EU citizens should carry a European Health Insurance Card (EHIC).

## Insider Tips

1. The car ferry is calmer and has more seating than a catamaran, which suits anyone with balance problems.
2. Walk the bay promenade in the morning, when shade falls across most of the western side.
3. Rent a car for one day only if the accommodation is far out. It costs less than repeated taxis, and the Split ferry takes the car for €35.60–€47.60.
4. Ask the accommodation host to meet you at the port, since many local hosts do this as a courtesy.

faq.question: Is Stari Grad suitable for elderly travelers?
faq.answer: Yes, for seniors who can walk slowly for 1–2 km. The old town and waterfront are mostly flat, though polished stone paving is slippery and few historic buildings have ramps. Visit in spring or autumn to avoid heat.

faq.question: Is Stari Grad wheelchair accessible?
faq.answer: Partly. The Riva waterfront and promenade are workable, but cobbled side lanes, thresholds and steps limit access. Tvrdalj has limited wheelchair access, so check with the venue and book accommodation with a step-free entrance.

faq.question: How do seniors get from Split to Stari Grad?
faq.answer: The Jadrolinija car ferry (line 635) takes 1 h 50 min and costs €5.90 in low season and €8.40 in high season per adult. The vehicle deck and ramp make boarding easier than on a catamaran.

faq.question: How far is the Stari Grad ferry port from the old town?
faq.answer: About 1.5 km, or a 20-minute walk. Seniors with luggage should pre-book a taxi, which typically costs €8–15, or arrange a pickup with their accommodation.

faq.question: What is the best month for seniors to visit Stari Grad?
faq.answer: May, June, September and early October are best, with temperatures of roughly 18–27°C. July and August often exceed 30°C and make midday walking hard.

faq.question: How much does it cost to enter Tvrdalj castle in Stari Grad?
faq.answer: Entry is €5 per person, paid in cash. Opening hours vary by season, with the morning slot from about 10:00 the most reliable, so check at the gate.

quickAnswer: Stari Grad suits seniors who walk slowly but steadily. The old town is compact and almost flat, with a 2 km waterfront promenade. Polished stone lanes get slippery, Tvrdalj has limited wheelchair access, and summer heat is the main risk. Visit April–June or September–October. The car ferry from Split takes 1 h 50 min.
